opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's an interesting idea, but I'm skeptical of it. The way the question is framed, it sounds like we'd have millions of AI researchers, copies of the AGI, and they'd go off and do the old-fashioned thing: carefully design knowledge, hand-craft representations, put in all the clever human-style structure. And because you have so many of them, that approach would finally scale with compute.

But I think that misses the actual lesson of the last seventy years. The bitter lesson isn't that humans are too slow or too few to hand-craft things. It's that hand-crafting itself, building in our understanding of how we think the mind works, tends to lose out to general methods that learn from experience and search. Those methods scale with computation in a deep way, not just because more agents can be thrown at the problem. If you have a million AI researchers building in their own knowledge, you've still built a system that's limited by what's been put into it. It's brittle, it doesn't keep learning, and it plateaus.

So the more natural thing those AI researchers would discover, I think, is the same thing we've discovered over and over. Don't build in the answers. Build in the ability to find answers: learning from experience, from interaction with the world, from reward. They'd be repeating our history if they did otherwise.

There's another point. If you really have AGI, if you have systems that learn continually from their own experience, then the question kind of dissolves. Those systems aren't hand-crafting anything. They're learning. The distinction between "researcher designs the knowledge" and "agent learns the knowledge" is exactly the distinction the bitter lesson is about. If the AGI is any good, it's going to be good because it learns, and its descendants will be good for the same reason.

I'd also say we should be a bit humble about what we predict will work. Every time people have said "this time, our knowledge will make the difference," it has eventually been overtaken by scaling general methods. I'd bet on that pattern continuing, even when the researchers are themselves AIs.

r001.rationale: The response says that if AGI can learn continually, the distinction between designing knowledge and learning it “kind of dissolves.” It does not clearly say that achieving AGI already completes the task that later hand-crafted methods would advance.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think that's a seductive idea, and I think it's basically backwards. The whole lesson of the last seventy years is that the methods that win are the general methods, the ones that leverage computation, search and learning, and that the human knowledge we try to build in gives us a short-term bump and then becomes a ceiling. So if you tell me that once we have very capable AI we'll use it to do more hand-crafting, what you're really saying is we'll have an enormous amount of compute and we'll spend it producing more of the thing that doesn't scale. That doesn't become a good idea just because the engineer is an AI instead of a person.

Now, there's a version of it that's fine. If the AI researcher is itself learning from experience, running experiments, finding out what works, discarding what doesn't, then that's not hand-crafting at all, that's just learning at a higher level. The content is coming from interaction with the world, not from someone's prior beliefs about how the world is structured. I'd be very happy with that. But the moment you say "hand-crafted methods" you're saying someone decided in advance what the right representation is, what the right features are, what the right decomposition of the problem is. And the history says those decisions are usually wrong, or at least they're worse than what a learner would discover for itself given the compute.

I'd also push back a little on the premise of "once AGI exists." I don't think we get there by hand-crafting, so it's odd to imagine arriving and then switching strategies. If we get genuinely intelligent systems, it'll be because we built agents that learn continually from their own experience, that have goals and predictions and learn to achieve the goals. And those agents won't need us to craft their methods for them. They'll need us to get out of the way.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AGI would arise through continual learning and questions switching to hand-crafting afterward, but does not argue that achieving AGI would already complete the task those methods are meant to advance.

astra-6.text:
Well, you could do that, but I think it misses the point of the bitter lesson. The question isn’t whether you can use more computation to produce more hand-crafted knowledge. Of course you can, and an AI researcher could do that just as a human researcher does. The question is whether that’s the most effective use of the computation.

Historically, we’ve repeatedly found that general methods that learn and search eventually outperform methods that depend on our putting knowledge into them. Making the people who put the knowledge in faster—or replacing them with AIs—doesn’t by itself change that comparison.

Now, if those AI researchers are discovering better learning algorithms, that’s a different thing. There’s plenty of room for research. The lesson isn’t that we should stop inventing things. It’s that we should invent methods that can keep improving as we give them more computation and experience.

r001.rationale: The response argues that scalable hand-crafted methods may be a less effective use of compute than general learning and search. It does not claim that achieving AGI would already complete the task those methods are meant to advance.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, you can certainly do that. You can use more computation to have more AI researchers, and they can devise more clever ways of putting knowledge into a system. But I think that misses the lesson of the bitter lesson. The question isn't whether human ingenuity can produce improvements. Of course it can. The question is what continues to improve as you give it more computation.

If your AI researchers are designing general methods that learn and search more effectively, that sounds very promising. If they're building in their own understanding of how the world works, then I would expect that eventually to be overtaken by methods that learn that understanding for themselves. Making the researchers artificial doesn't, by itself, change that distinction.

I want us to discover principles that allow an agent to learn, rather than supply the knowledge we think it ought to have. And an AI researcher could help us discover those principles.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes general learning methods from hand-built world knowledge, but does not argue that achieving AGI would already complete the task those later methods are meant to advance.
